stem: Neither the manager nor the employees ______ aware of the new policy.
solutionSteps: With 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject.
The nearer subject is 'the employees' — plural.
So the plural 'were' is correct.

trapExplanations.1: Agrees with 'the manager', the further subject — the rule uses the nearer one.
trapExplanations.2: Singular and also shifts the tense out of the sentence's past frame.
trapExplanations.3: Singular present perfect; both the number and the aspect are wrong here.

stem: By the time the results ______ published, the team had already moved on to the next study.
solutionSteps: The main clause uses 'had already moved' — past perfect.
Past perfect marks the earlier of two past events, so the other clause must be simple past.
'Were published' is the correct passive simple past.

trapExplanations.1: Present perfect cannot pair with past perfect in this construction.
trapExplanations.2: Future tense contradicts 'had already moved on'.
trapExplanations.3: Simple present clashes with the past narrative frame.

stem: The findings, ______ were published last year, have since been widely cited.
solutionSteps: The clause is set off by commas, making it non-restrictive — extra information.
Non-restrictive clauses about things take 'which', never 'that'.
'Which' is correct.

trapExplanations.1: 'That' introduces restrictive clauses and cannot follow a comma. The most common error in this pattern.
trapExplanations.3: 'What' cannot introduce a relative clause modifying a stated noun.

stem: ______ more carefully, the experiment might have produced usable data.
solutionSteps: 'Might have produced' signals an unreal past conditional.
The inverted form 'Had it been ...' is the standard way to open such a clause without 'if'.
It is also passive, which the experiment (the thing designed) requires.

trapExplanations.1: Wrong voice and tense — the experiment did not design anything.
trapExplanations.2: A dangling participle: it would make the experiment the one doing the designing.
trapExplanations.3: 'Unless' reverses the logic and does not fit the counterfactual.

stem: The report recommends that each department ______ its budget by the end of the quarter.
solutionSteps: 'Recommend that' triggers the subjunctive mood in English.
The subjunctive uses the bare infinitive regardless of the subject.
So 'submit', not 'submits'.

trapExplanations.1: The ordinary third-person singular form, which the subjunctive overrides. This is the trap the item is built on.
trapExplanations.2: Past tense does not fit a recommendation about future action.
trapExplanations.3: 'Will' is not used in subjunctive that-clauses after 'recommend'.

stem: The report, along with its appendices, ______ been sent to every member of the committee.
solutionSteps: Strip out the phrase between the commas: 'along with its appendices' is not part of the subject.
The subject left behind is 'the report' — singular.
A singular subject takes 'has'.

trapExplanations.1: Agrees with 'appendices', which sits inside a phrase and cannot be the subject.
trapExplanations.2: Plural and past simple; neither fits a singular subject before 'been'.
trapExplanations.3: Plural, and 'are been' is not a possible form.

stem: If she ______ half an hour earlier, she would have caught the last train.
solutionSteps: The main clause uses 'would have caught' — a third conditional about the unreal past.
The if-clause of a third conditional takes the past perfect.
'Had left' is the past perfect.

trapExplanations.1: Past simple belongs to the second conditional, which pairs with 'would catch'.
trapExplanations.2: 'Would' does not belong in the if-clause of a conditional.
trapExplanations.3: Present perfect cannot describe an unreal past situation.

stem: Neither of the two proposals ______ acceptable to the board in its present form.
solutionSteps: The subject is 'neither', not 'proposals' — 'of the two proposals' is a prepositional phrase.
'Neither' is treated as singular.
The singular past form is 'was'.

trapExplanations.1: Agrees with 'proposals' inside the prepositional phrase rather than with the subject.
trapExplanations.2: Plural, and it also shifts the tense away from the past frame.
trapExplanations.3: Plural and present, wrong on both counts.

stem: Hardly ______ the meeting begun when the fire alarm went off.
solutionSteps: 'Hardly' at the start of a clause forces inversion of subject and auxiliary.
The pattern is 'hardly had X done Y when Z' — past perfect for the earlier event.
'Had' is the auxiliary the past perfect needs.

trapExplanations.1: Present perfect clashes with 'went off', which is past.
trapExplanations.2: 'Did' cannot be followed by the past participle 'begun'.
trapExplanations.3: 'Was begun' is passive, but the meeting began by itself here.

stem: She is one of those managers who ______ always willing to listen.
solutionSteps: Ask what 'who' refers back to: 'those managers', not 'one'.
The relative clause therefore has a plural subject.
'Are' agrees with 'those managers'.

trapExplanations.1: Agrees with 'one', but 'who' attaches to the plural noun immediately before it.
trapExplanations.2: Singular and past; the sentence is in the present.
trapExplanations.3: Singular present perfect, so both the number and the aspect are off.
